stem: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, blood sugar rises above the normal range. Which of the following islet responses most directly lowers that concentration?

options.label: A
options.text: Alpha-cell glucagon release mobilizing hepatic glycogen
options.misconception: The fasting (glucose-raising) response is being applied to the fed state.
options.explanation: Glucagon raises blood glucose; after a meal the needed response is insulin release, not glucagon.

options.label: B
options.text: Delta-cell somatostatin release blocking all islet hormones
options.misconception: A non-selective inhibitory peptide is being treated as the primary fed-state actuator.
options.explanation: Somatostatin can inhibit insulin and glucagon, but the direct glucose-lowering response to hyperglycemia is beta-cell insulin secretion.

options.label: C
options.text: Beta-cell insulin release promoting cellular glucose uptake
options.misconception: None; elevated glucose stimulates beta cells to release insulin, which drives glucose into target cells.
options.explanation: Elevated blood glucose stimulates beta-cell insulin release; insulin facilitates glucose uptake into body cells and thereby lowers blood glucose.

options.label: D
options.text: PP-cell polypeptide release reducing further food intake
options.misconception: An appetite signal is being substituted for the acute glycemic response.
options.explanation: Pancreatic polypeptide may affect appetite; it does not lower a postprandial glucose rise the way insulin does.

options.label: E
options.text: Acinar-cell enzyme release accelerating intestinal digestion
options.misconception: Exocrine digestion is being confused with endocrine glucose disposal.
options.explanation: Acinar enzymes aid digestion but do not lower blood glucose; that is the role of insulin from beta cells.

context: Learning objective: apply the fed-state islet response. Rising blood glucose stimulates beta-cell insulin release; insulin promotes cellular glucose uptake and storage, lowering concentration. Glucagon is the opposing (fasting) response.
